CausalChain: Oxidative stress in liver cells -> Nrf2 dissociation from Keap1 -> Enhanced p62 phosphorylation (selectively via nanoparticle delivery) -> p62 binds Keap1 -> Autophagic degradation of Keap1 -> Controlled Nrf2 nuclear translocation (monitored by real-time omics/imaging) -> Upregulation of cytoprotective antioxidant genes -> Suppression of hepatic stellate cell activation -> Attenuation of liver fibrosis
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that employing a nanoparticle-based, liver stellate cell-targeted drug delivery system to pharmacologically enhance p62 phosphorylation will specifically induce autophagic degradation of Keap1, thereby triggering a tightly controlled activation of Nrf2. This controlled activation, continuously monitored through integrated omics and imaging approaches, will upregulate antioxidant defenses, reduce oxidative stress, and suppress hepatic stellate cell activation, ultimately mitigating liver fibrosis. This strategy aims to circumvent the oncogenic risks of chronic, systemic Nrf2 activation by confining the modulation effect to hepatic stellate cells and maintaining Nrf2 activity within an optimized therapeutic window.
Abstract: We propose that a targeted, nanoparticle-mediated delivery system can be engineered to selectively enhance p62 phosphorylation in hepatic stellate cells, thereby promoting precise Keap1 degradation and controlled Nrf2 activation. This approach is designed to restore the oxidative balance by upregulating cytoprotective antioxidant genes while suppressing hepatic stellate cell activation and attenuating liver fibrosis. In contrast to conventional, systemic Nrf2 activators that risk oncogenesis through chronic, non-specific activation, our strategy employs real-time omics monitoring and imaging to dynamically calibrate Nrf2 activity within a safe therapeutic window. This targeted intervention leverages contemporary nanotechnology and multi-omics to achieve high specificity and robust control over the p62–Keap1–Nrf2 pathway, leading to improved therapeutic outcomes in liver fibrogenesis without off‐target effects.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis suggested selective pharmacological enhancement of p62 phosphorylation in hepatic stellate cells to promote Keap1 degradation and trigger controlled Nrf2 activation. The revised hypothesis builds on this causal chain by incorporating modern technological advances, namely, the development of nanoparticle-based targeted drug delivery systems that ensure cell-type specificity, and the integration of real-time omics and imaging technologies to rigorously monitor and control Nrf2 activation. Each step of the original causal chain is maintained, from oxidative stress-induced signaling to attenuation of liver fibrosis, but the revised hypothesis addresses key issues related to specificity, dosage, and off-target effects, thus enhancing both the novelty and practical implementability of the intervention.
